c1.story:
Stand at any traffic signal in India and count. A swarm of motorcycles and scooters at the front, a few cars and SUVs behind them, an autorickshaw squeezing through, a truck idling at the back, maybe a tractor on the shoulder if you are outside a city. Every one of those machines came out of a listed company's plant, and every one of them was bought by a very different customer for a very different reason.

That is the first thing to understand about the automobile sector: the index moves as one block, but the businesses inside it do not. A Hero Splendor is bought by a young man in a district town who needs to get to work and whose family's cash depends on the harvest. A Mahindra Scorpio is bought by a salaried professional in Pune on a five-year loan, after weeks of comparing features on YouTube. A Tata or Ashok Leyland truck is bought by a fleet owner who has done the maths on freight rates and diesel and decided this is the month to add capacity. A replacement tyre is bought by anyone whose old one has worn out, which happens whether or not the economy feels good.

So the same piece of news lands differently on each door. A repo rate cut lowers car instalments within weeks. A good monsoon fills rural wallets and shows up in motorcycle and tractor sales around harvest and Diwali. A burst of highway and mining spending puts trucks on order. A spike in natural rubber prices only really hurts the tyre makers.

The auto index is four businesses holding hands. They let go the moment the cycle turns.

Some companies straddle doors. Mahindra sells SUVs, tractors and light commercial vehicles under one roof; Eicher owns Royal Enfield motorcycles and a truck joint venture with Volvo. That is fine. It just means you think about the pieces separately, because a weak tractor season and a hot SUV launch can arrive in the same quarter.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, then compare across.

  • The name and the line under it tell you who the customer is and where the margin comes from: scale and spares for bikes, model mix and discipline on discounts for cars, the freight and farm cycle for trucks and tractors, the replacement market for tyres.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Mahindra appears under two doors on purpose, since it sells both SUVs and tractors and light trucks.
  • The bar shows how much of the profit the company keeps rather than handing it to suppliers, dealers or customers. Notice something unusual here: all four bars sit at medium. No door in autos is a pure price taker and none is a toll booth. The difference between them is not how much they keep but what makes the amount swing.
  • The last line is the bet you are really making. Read the four side by side and you get four different macro exposures: rural cash and petrol, loan rates and the hit model, capex and freight, rubber against crude.

Below the tiles, the analogy and the so-what line make the point the bars cannot: because the profit kept looks similar, the thing to decide first is which cycle you want to own. Pick any auto stock and name its door before you look at a single valuation number.

c2.story:
Picture the industry as a long kitchen with five stations. At the back door, raw ingredients arrive: flat steel coils from Tata Steel and JSW, aluminium from Hindalco, copper, natural rubber, plastics and, for electric vehicles, lithium cells and the rare-earth magnets that sit inside every electric motor. At the front door, a finished vehicle drives out to a family, a fleet owner or a farmer, who will feed it fuel, servicing and spares for the next ten years.

In between, the cooking happens in stages. A huge and underrated component industry forges crankshafts, casts housings, wires harnesses and moulds dashboards. Then the assembler, the brand on the bonnet, bolts thousands of those parts together on a line where the scale of the plant decides the cost of each vehicle. Then dealers sell it and banks and NBFCs lend against it, because most vehicles in India leave the showroom on a loan.

Here is the part people miss. The listed carmakers and bikemakers stand at only one station, assembly. They buy from steelmakers who have the upper hand, and they sell through dealers and lenders they need. Their genius, when they have it, is in scale, in design and in squeezing the stations on either side.

And the rival at the back door is not who you would expect. China sells almost no cars in India. But it owns the electric supply chain: most of the world's battery cells and nearly all its processed rare-earth magnets. In April 2025 Beijing put rare-earth magnets under export licensing, and within weeks Indian electric lines were waiting for parts. Bajaj warned in the summer that its Chetak electric scooter output was being cut sharply, before supplies resumed in late August. That is what owning one station looks like: a decision in Beijing can stop a line in Pune.
c2.read:
The diagram has two layers. Read the five boxes left to right, then drop down to the band row.

The five boxes run from raw materials on the left to the owner and the aftermarket on the right. Under each name you see what happens there and who stands there. Notice how the cast changes: metal companies and China on the left, an army of component makers next, the familiar listed brands in the middle, then dealers and lenders, then households, fleets and farmers.

The band row says who holds each station. Only one cell, assembly, is coloured as India listed. The first cell is marked as a rival station because China sits there for cells and magnets alongside Indian metal. The rest are other people's territory: suppliers, dealers, lenders, owners. The replacement tyre makers appear in the last box's who line, a reminder that the aftermarket is where the tyre door earns its fat margins.

Use the row as a map of where shocks come from.

  • A steel or rubber price move starts at station one and reaches the assembler's margin about a quarter later.
  • A Chinese magnet or cell curb also starts at station one but stops an electric line at once, with no lag at all.
  • A credit squeeze starts at station four and travels backwards, as it did when NBFC lending froze in 2019.

The note below the boxes tells you where the plants cluster, and the so-what line spells out why supply, not demand, has been the recent bottleneck.

c3.story:
Who actually buys a vehicle in India? Not one customer, but eight very different ones, each listening to a different drumbeat.

The urban household buying a car or a premium motorcycle is mostly watching its monthly instalment, its tax bill and the price at the petrol pump. That is why the February 2025 budget, which made incomes up to twelve lakh rupees effectively tax-free under the new regime, and the GST cut that followed in September, landed together like a double espresso for car demand.

The rural household buying a commuter bike or a small car is watching the sky. A good monsoon means a good kharif crop, which means cash at harvest, which means Splendors and Shines leaving showrooms in October and November. In 2019 and again through much of 2021 and 2022, rural incomes lagged and entry motorcycles had a miserable run even while SUVs had waiting lists.

Fleet owners are cold-blooded. They buy trucks when freight rates are firm, diesel is manageable and their existing trucks are running full. Farmers buy tractors when reservoirs are full and crop support prices are generous. State transport corporations buy buses, increasingly electric, when the budget and subsidy schemes allow. Delivery and ride-hailing operators buy three-wheelers and electric scooters by the thousand when gig demand is strong.

Then there are the customers abroad: Bajaj and TVS ship motorcycles to Africa and Latin America, and that trade lives and dies on whether those countries have dollars. When Nigeria's naira crashed in 2023, Bajaj's export volumes took a heavy knock. And finally the replacement buyer, who buys tyres, batteries and spares simply because the vehicle on the road is ageing.

The practical lesson: an auto stock's next quarter is usually visible in somebody else's data first.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy: cars, entry bikes, trucks, buses, three-wheelers, export motorcycles, tractors, or tyres and spares.
  • The third line is what moves them. This is your watch list outside the auto sector: loan rates and GST for urban buyers, the monsoon and crop prices for rural ones, freight and road capex for fleets, dollar availability in Africa for exports.

A good way to use the grid is to pin each tile to a door from card one. Urban households map to the passenger-vehicle door and premium bikes. Rural households and farmers map to two-wheelers and tractors. Fleet operators and state transport map to commercial vehicles. Replacement buyers map to tyres. Once you have done that, a single headline tells you which door it touches.

Notice the tiles that move on something other than Indian income: export markets move on foreign currency and tariffs, and ride-hailing moves on electric subsidies and city permits. These are the tiles that can surprise you when the domestic picture looks calm.

The so-what line below compresses the whole grid into one habit: a monsoon headline is a bike and tractor signal, a rate cut is a car signal, and a freight-rate chart is a truck signal.

c4.story:
Strip an automaker down and it is a giant spread business. It buys steel, aluminium, rubber and thousands of bought-out parts at whatever the market charges, and sells the finished vehicle at a sticker price it changes only a couple of times a year. The gap between those two is the whole game, and it is a narrower gap than most people imagine.

Why so narrow? Because the assembler adds surprisingly little of the physical value itself. Most of what is inside a Maruti Swift or a TVS Jupiter was made by a supplier. The carmaker's value lies in design, scale, the brand and the dealer network. That means raw materials and parts swallow the large majority of every rupee of sales, and a few points of commodity inflation can wipe out a large share of what is left.

The timing makes it worse. Steel prices move every month; vehicle prices move twice a year at most, because a carmaker that raises prices mid-season hands customers to its rivals. So when metal spikes, margins shrink first and the price hike arrives a quarter later. You saw this vividly in 2021, when steel prices soared and carmakers' margins were squeezed for several quarters before price hikes caught up.

Then there is the line that hides in plain sight: discounts. They are buried inside net sales, so you never see a discount line, you only see revenue per vehicle falling. In 2022 and 2023, with SUV waiting lists stretching for months, discounts nearly vanished and margins hit records. By 2024, dealer stock had piled up and discounts were back.

The best auto quarter is not the one with the most vehicles sold. It is the one with the fewest discounts given.

Two quieter lines matter at the biggest names. Maruti and Hyundai India pay a royalty to their Japanese and Korean parents on every car. And cash piles at Maruti, Bajaj and Hero earn treasury income that is a meaningful slice of reported profit.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a two-wheeler maker and a passenger-vehicle maker. Start at the left of each chart and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is raw materials and bought-out parts. It is enormous in both charts: roughly seven of every ten rupees for bikes and close to three quarters for cars. That is the assembler's position in the kitchen made visible.
  • The opex bar is people, marketing, dealer incentives and warranty. It is similar in both, a little larger for cars.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is thin for both, slightly thicker for cars, which need bigger plants and more expensive tooling per model.
  • The last bar is what is left. Bikes keep roughly an eighth of each rupee, cars a little under a tenth. Small differences in the input bar create big differences here.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the list marks the lines that matter. Four get a clear yes: gross margin, discounts and dealer incentives, depreciation, and capex with asset turn. The other four get a sometimes. Notice that none gets a no: in autos, even royalty and treasury income can move the reported number. Working capital is flagged as sometimes for a reason worth remembering: makers collect from dealers faster than they pay suppliers, so the stock to watch is not at the factory but at the dealer.

c5.story:
Vehicles are the second-biggest purchase most Indian households ever make, after a home, and most are bought on credit. That makes the sector cyclical in the old-fashioned way: when credit, income and confidence line up, everyone buys at once, and when one of them cracks, everyone waits.

The last full cycle is a textbook. From 2016 to 2018 credit was easy, new SUVs kept launching and rural incomes recovered. Then, in September 2018, IL&FS defaulted and the NBFCs that financed a huge share of vehicle purchases, especially trucks and two-wheelers, stopped lending almost overnight. Around the same time, new rules made multi-year third-party insurance compulsory at purchase, raising the upfront cost, and revised axle-load norms let existing trucks carry more, so fleets needed fewer new ones. On top of that, the industry was racing to jump straight from BS-IV to BS-VI emission norms by April 2020. Truck sales collapsed, and then Covid emptied showrooms entirely.

The recovery came in a strange order. Personal mobility came first, because nobody wanted to ride a crowded bus in 2020, but the chip shortage capped how many cars could be built. Then the SUV boom of 2022 and 2023: Mahindra's Thar and Scorpio-N and Maruti's Brezza and Grand Vitara had waiting lists, discounts disappeared, margins hit records. Two-wheelers lagged until rural incomes caught up in 2024.

Then came 2025, the year policy lit the fuse. The GST overhaul that took effect in late September moved small cars and bikes up to a certain engine size from the top slab to the middle one, while bigger cars and large motorcycles moved to a new top slab. Combined with the income-tax relief earlier in the year, it produced the strongest festive season in years.

Which leaves the industry where the clock now points: in the boom, at record volumes, with a high base to beat next year.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each arc belong to the last full cycle: boom from 2016 to 2018, the peak in 2018, the bust through 2019 and 2020, the bottom in 2020. The arrow points to today, and it sits inside the boom arc, labelled as a policy-fuelled upswing with record volumes and a high base. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase last time.

The timeline runs from 2019 to now and is colour-coded by tone. Read it top to bottom: two bust entries, the SUV boom, a neutral and sluggish 2024, a boom year in 2025 and the entry marked now. The story is a long climb out of a credit-and-Covid hole that got a sharp policy kick at the end.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Dealer inventory: lean, arrow up. Lean stock means pricing power; above six weeks means discounts are coming.
  • Retail against wholesale: retail ahead, arrow up. Customers are buying faster than factories are shipping, the healthy way round.
  • Steel, aluminium and rubber: firming, arrow down. This is the hand working against the boom, pressing on margins until the next price hike.
  • Loan rates and NBFC disbursals: easing, arrow up.

Three hands help and one hurts. That matches the call: still healthy, but late.

c6.story:
An automaker's results are shaped by people who will never set foot in its showrooms. A monetary policy committee in Mumbai. A GST Council of finance ministers in Delhi. Steel traders. The India Meteorological Department. And, lately, a commerce ministry official in Beijing issuing magnet export licences.

What makes autos unusual is how many of those dials carry real weight. In most sectors, one or two outside forces dominate. Here, four can make or break a year on their own: interest rates, steel and aluminium prices, the monsoon and tax policy.

Interest rates work through the instalment. A carmaker is really selling a monthly payment, and when the RBI cuts, as it did repeatedly through 2025, that payment falls and fence-sitters turn into buyers within a couple of quarters. Trucks are even more rate-sensitive, because fleet owners borrow for nearly the whole price. The monsoon works through rural cash, reaching bikes and tractors around harvest and the festive season. Steel and aluminium work through the spread, squeezing margins until prices are reset. And tax policy works through the sticker price itself: the September 2025 GST cut moved the price of an entry car or commuter bike more in one day than most companies' own price changes manage in years.

In autos the government is not a regulator in the background. It is a dial on the dashboard.

Then there are the two-faced dials. A weaker rupee helps Bajaj and TVS, which earn dollars from exports, and hurts anyone importing parts or paying a royalty abroad. Crude oil hurts petrol bike buyers and the tyre makers, but nudges buyers towards electric. And the slow ones: Chinese export controls on magnets and cells, foreign tariffs and trade deals, which decide how much of the electric future gets built here.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: the route by which it reaches profits. For autos, read this column carefully, because several dials work through the buyer, not the factory: the monthly instalment, rural cash, the sticker price.
  • A rise does: a green upward arrow means a rise helps, a red downward arrow means it hurts, a diamond means it depends on the company. Here the reds dominate: rates, metal, crude, tax and Chinese controls all hurt when they rise. The greens are the monsoon, freight and infrastructure capex, and consumer durables output.
  • Weight: one to three dots.

Count the three-dot rows: there are four. Interest rates, steel and aluminium, the monsoon, and GST and income-tax policy. That is a lot of heavy dials for one sector, and it explains why autos react to so many different headlines.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track: the money market rate for interest rates, core-sector steel output for metal, food inflation as a monsoon proxy, Brent crude, the rupee, the infrastructure index, consumer durables output. Policy and trade dials show a dash, because there is no single number for a GST Council decision or a Beijing licence; for those you read the news.

The so-what line tells you to watch two dials if you watch nothing else: loan rates for cars and trucks, the monsoon for bikes and tractors.

c7.story:
India builds more two-wheelers than anyone and is the third-largest car market in the world. So why do its automakers not command the returns their scale suggests? The bottlenecks answer that.

Start with the two that never go away. The first is that the electric supply chain belongs to China. Cells, magnets and much of the power electronics are imported, and 2025 showed what that means: when Beijing tightened licences on rare-earth magnets, Indian electric scooter lines ran at a fraction of plan for weeks. The second is that technology at the two biggest carmakers is rented. Maruti pays Suzuki and Hyundai India pays its Korean parent a royalty on every car, so a slice of every sale leaves the country before Indian shareholders see it.

Then come the recurring traps. Channel stuffing is the oldest trick in the industry: makers report wholesale dispatches to dealers, not retail sales to customers, so a slowing market can be hidden for a quarter or two by pushing stock into showrooms. The dealers' association has complained about this more than once, most loudly in 2024 when unsold car stock piled up. Regulatory step-ups arrive on fixed dates: BS-VI, airbag and braking mandates, crash testing, fuel-economy targets. Each one lifts costs in a single step. And part shortages, chips in 2021 and magnets in 2025, can idle a line however strong demand is.

The cyclical ones are about timing. Steel reprices monthly while vehicles reprice twice a year, so every metal spike costs a quarter of margin. And trucks amplify everything: fleets buy in bursts and trucks last a decade, so a mild freight slowdown can halve truck sales, as it did in 2019.

Finally the slow one: the electric switch in scooters, where incumbents have lost share to newcomers like Ather and Ola Electric, which in turn have struggled to make money.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, a plain reason why it bites, and a severity label. The label tells you how to treat it.

  • Structural: permanent, so it belongs in your valuation. For autos these are the top two, China's grip on the electric supply chain and royalties to foreign parents.
  • Recurring: comes back again and again. There are three here: channel stuffing, regulatory step-ups and chip or part shortages. These are the headlines that move a single stock for a week, or a quarter.
  • Cyclical: bites at turning points. The commodity pass-through lag and the truck cycle's amplitude sit here.
  • Slow: grinding change, not a shock. The electric transition in two-wheelers is the only slow one, but it is the one that decides which incumbents look different in ten years.

Read the table in the order the so-what line suggests. The first two cap returns for good, so you should not expect any automaker to earn the margins of a software company. The third and fifth rows, channel stuffing and part shortages, are the quarter-level surprises worth a news alert per company. A practical test for channel stuffing: compare the company's monthly dispatches with the registration data published from the government's vehicle portal. When dispatches run well ahead of registrations for more than a couple of months, the dealer is carrying the slowdown for the maker.

c8.story:
In most industries, the regulator sits in the background. In autos it sits in the driver's seat, and it changes the price of the product, its design and who can sell it.

Take tax. The GST Council decides what share of a vehicle's price goes to the government, and in September 2025 it made the biggest change in a decade: small petrol and diesel cars under four metres and motorcycles up to a certain engine size dropped from the top slab to the middle one, while larger cars and big motorcycles, including Royal Enfield's larger twins, moved up to a new top slab. Overnight, entry vehicles got meaningfully cheaper and the festive season exploded.

Then the road transport ministry. It sets emission norms, safety rules and crash testing. The jump from BS-IV straight to BS-VI in April 2020 added real cost to every engine, and the Supreme Court refused to let unsold BS-IV vehicles be registered after the deadline, leaving dealers scrambling. Bharat NCAP, launched in 2023, turned crash ratings into a marketing weapon; Tata and Mahindra have used five-star scores as a selling point.

The heavy industries ministry hands out electric subsidies, first FAME, now PM E-DRIVE, and the design of each scheme has decided who wins the electric scooter race. When subsidies were cut sharply in mid-2023, prices rose and volumes stalled. The petroleum ministry's ethanol blending programme, which reached a fifth of petrol in 2025, brought a wave of mileage complaints from owners of older vehicles. And the electric car import scheme cut duties for foreign makers that commit to a local plant, which is part of why Tesla opened showrooms in 2025 and VinFast opened a plant in Tamil Nadu.

Behind them all sits the RBI, because without vehicle finance this industry simply stops.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and status.

The status column is how to prioritise.

  • Always: the road transport ministry, the RBI and the Competition Commission. Permanent fixtures. The ministry's norms arrive on fixed dates, so you can see the cost step-ups coming years ahead.
  • Live: actively shaping volumes now. Electric subsidies, the ethanol mandate and the scrappage policy sit here. Subsidy design is the one to watch for anyone owning an electric scooter maker.
  • New: the GST overhaul and the electric car import scheme. The GST change is the most important row on this card for the next year, because the industry will be lapping its effect.
  • Coming: the next phase of CAFE fuel-economy norms. This pushes carmakers towards hybrids and electrics or penalties, and it will shape model mix and capex plans.

Notice the pattern down the why column: almost every row either moves the sticker price or adds a cost step. That is why autos react to policy headlines more than most consumer sectors.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces ask one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Rivals can start a discount war, suppliers can squeeze input prices, buyers can bargain, newcomers can crowd in and substitutes can make the product less needed.

Run passenger vehicles through the test. Rivalry is intense: a dozen carmakers launch new models every year, and the leader's grip on the market has loosened as Mahindra, Tata, Hyundai and Toyota pushed into SUVs. When a segment gets crowded, discounts follow. But entry is hard: a car plant costs thousands of crores and a national dealer network takes a decade. The government's electric import scheme is the main crack in that wall.

Now two-wheelers. For decades this looked like the better business: four big players, Hero, Honda, Bajaj and TVS, plus Royal Enfield in its own niche, with fat margins and huge cash piles. Then electric scooters arrived and blew the entry barrier open. Starting an electric scooter company needed no engine know-how and no century-old supply base, and with subsidies flowing, a dozen startups entered. Ather and Ola Electric took share from incumbents. Electric scooters are also a direct substitute for petrol bikes, and bike buyers are famously price-sensitive.

Electric did not change how many two-wheelers India buys. It changed who is allowed to sell them.

Suppliers sit in the middle for both. Component makers are many and depend on the assemblers, which gives the carmaker leverage. But steel mills and Chinese magnet and cell makers have the upper hand, which is why the supplier score is moderate rather than low.

The verdict from the forces: carmakers with a hit SUV and lean dealers keep the profit this cycle, and two-wheeler incumbents keep theirs where newcomers have not yet arrived, in entry motorcycles and exports.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn, passenger vehicles and two-wheelers. Look at overall size first. The shapes are close, and neither reaches the outer ring of three on any spoke: autos is a decent business, not a broken one.

Now look at where they differ.

  • Rivalry: cars reach further. A crowded model battle is harder than a four-player bike market.
  • Suppliers: identical. Both face the same steel mills and the same Chinese electric chain.
  • Buyers: two-wheelers reach further, because bike buyers count every rupee.
  • Entrants: the biggest gap on the chart. Two-wheelers reach well out; cars stay tucked in. This one spoke is the electric scooter story.
  • Substitutes: two-wheelers reach a little further, with electric scooters substituting for petrol bikes.

Here is the surprise worth noticing: the two-wheeler shape is the larger of the two overall, even though bikemakers have historically earned better returns. The chart is telling you the future pressure, not past profits.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a one-line reason. If you own a specific company, redraw its shape in your head: Royal Enfield's premium niche or an exporter's African market would shrink the entrants and buyer spokes considerably.

c10.story:
An auto results call is full of model names, launch calendars and capacity plans. Most of it is colour. Eight numbers tell you whether the quarter was genuinely good, and whether the next one will be.

Start with volumes and market share by segment, because they tell you whether the company is winning its door. A maker growing slower than its segment is losing, however good the headline growth looks. Pair that with the gap between retail registrations and wholesale dispatches; if dispatches run ahead, the growth is sitting in dealer yards.

Then the margin pair. Gross margin is pricing power against steel and rubber. EBITDA margin layers on operating leverage: a full plant spreads its fixed costs over more vehicles, so margins can jump sharply when volumes rise. Watch them together through a metal spike to see who passes costs on quickly.

Next, the discount detectors. Dealer inventory days tell you whether discounts are coming; under a month for cars is healthy, more than six weeks is a warning. Average realisation per vehicle tells you about mix and discounting at once: rising realisation without volume loss means customers are buying up, to SUVs or premium bikes, and paying full price.

Then the build numbers: capex against depreciation, with asset turn. Automakers are adding capacity again; Maruti's new Haryana plant and the foreign makers' pledges are examples. Capacity added into strong demand is fine, but asset turn should stay high or the expansion was premature.

Finally, inventory days at the maker, which flag part shortages or stuffed plants, and return on capital, which tells you whether the whole machine earns more than it costs to fund across a full cycle. The best Indian two-wheeler and car makers have historically cleared that bar comfortably.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company you own.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, and in autos it often gives separate marks for cars, bikes and trucks. Read the mark for the right door: a truck maker's margin will never look like a two-wheeler's, and it should not be judged against one.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It appears for gross margin, EBITDA margin, capex to depreciation, inventory days and return on capital.

Three rows show a dash in the median column: volumes and share, dealer inventory days and realisation per vehicle. They are not in annual filings. For those you go to monthly sources: company sales releases on the first of each month, registration data from the government's vehicle portal, and the dealers' association's monthly report.

The way to use the table: for any company, compare three things, its own number, the median and the good mark. Then check the two leading rows, dealer inventory and realisation, before the margin rows, because they tell you where margin is heading rather than where it has been.

c11.story:
The best early warnings about auto earnings rarely come from automakers' own calls. They come from the dealers' association's monthly registration data, from the RBI's policy statements, from steel price trackers, from toll collection numbers on highways, from the monsoon map in July, and lately from licensing notices in Beijing.

Each speaks with a different lead time. Registrations and Chinese licence decisions tell you about this quarter. Loan rates, steel and rubber, freight rates and tolls, fuel prices and tax decisions speak about a quarter ahead. The monsoon speaks two quarters ahead: farm cash in autumn is bike and tractor sales at harvest and the festive season.

Combine them and you get a simple three-part test. The sector is in a genuine up-cycle when retail registrations run ahead of wholesale dispatches, dealer inventory is lean, and gross margins are expanding against steel. Right now two of those are true. Festive retail demand after the GST cut was real, not dispatches stuffed into showrooms, and dealer stock is comfortably under six weeks. The missing sign is margin: metal prices are firming and the price hikes that would offset them have not yet landed.

That is why the call reads late boom, still healthy. The demand is genuine, the channel is clean, but the easy margin gains are behind us and the base for next year's comparison is high. Within the sector, the call leans towards carmakers with lean dealers and a strong SUV mix and towards two-wheeler exporters, and is wary of trucks at peak margins and of electric scooter makers that still lose money.

The risk to watch is not demand. It is supply, China's grip on magnets and cells, and the temptation to stuff dealers to flatter a quarter once growth slows.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel through which it reaches earnings.

  • Far left, same quarter: monthly retail registrations and Chinese export licences for magnets and cells.
  • One quarter ahead: the crowded middle, with loan rates and NBFC disbursals, steel and rubber, freight and tolls, fuel prices, and budget and GST decisions.
  • Two quarters ahead: the monsoon and kharif sowing, the earliest warning on the chart.

Use it as a reading order. Each July, check the monsoon dot first, because it tells you about the festive quarter. Each month, check the middle dots. The left-hand dots tell you what is already happening.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. Two ticks: retail ahead of wholesale, with festive demand real, and dealer inventory lean, under six weeks. One cross: gross margins are not expanding, because metal is firming and price hikes are pending. Two of three is what the rule calls a healthy upswing.

The call box gives the directional view, the three points behind it, and what would change it: dealer stock climbing past six weeks with discounts, a metal spike without price hikes, or rates turning up and a weak monsoon. Treat those as alerts. If any appears in the monthly data, the call is due for a rethink.
